claims.text: The US legalized gay marriage only 10 years ago.
Candidates in other countries will be able to use anti‑LGBT rhetoric for a considerably longer time.

implicit_assumptions: Legalization timelines in one country imply similar or longer delays elsewhere.
The presence of social media influences the duration of anti‑LGBT rhetoric.
Persistence of anti‑LGBT rhetoric is directly tied to policy change timelines.
scope_notes: No specific countries identified; generalizes from the US to other nations.
Timeframe of persistence is not quantified.
uncertainty: Speculative and based on unverified extrapolation.

Inference.supporting_quote: The US just legalized gay marriage only 10 years ago.
Inference.structure_objection: The premise that the US legalized gay marriage 10 years ago does not logically entail that anti‑LGBT rhetoric will endure longer in other countries; the inference jumps from a single policy change to a global trend without evidence of causal link.
Inference.alternative_interpretation: The argument might be a speculative projection, but absent evidence, it commits a non‑sequitur reasoning flaw.

Evidence.supporting_quote: The US just legalized gay marriage only 10 years ago.
Evidence.structure_objection: The argument extrapolates a single case to all other jurisdictions without evidence, treating a specific policy timeline as representative of future timelines elsewhere.
Evidence.alternative_interpretation: The claim could be a speculative observation rather than a definitive claim, but the inference drawn (“Candidates in other countries will be able to use anti‑LGBT rhetoric for a considerably longer time”) remains unsupported by data.
